evidence.title: Correction: Explainable deep learning for healthcare workforce attrition: a methodological study on the Watson healthcare synthetic benchmark
evidence.abstract: Conclusion: On this synthetic benchmark, a compact interpretable deep network performs within one cross-fold standard deviation of strong tabular baselines-gradient boosting attains the highest mean AUC-ROC and AUC-PR, and the two strongest baselines retain a small, statistically significant ROC edge-while providing axiomatic, dual-level SHAP explanations that translate into three candidate retention levers: overtime reduction, working-environment improvement, and commuting support. Because the records are synthetic, these levers should be regarded as datadriven hypotheses rather than validated interventions, and prospective evaluation on real, deidentified hospital workforce data remains a necessary next step.The original version of this article has been updated.Contribution (1) erroneously read: "We demonstrated through 5-fold stratified cross-validation that this interpretable deep model attains predictive performance that is statistically comparable with and on the minority-class AUC-PR metric superior to strong tabular baselines, including logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting." A correction has been made to this passage:We demonstrate through 5-fold stratified cross-validation that this interpretable deep model attains predictive performance within one cross-fold standard deviation of strong tabular baselines including logistic regression, random forest and gradient boosting (under a leak-free crossvalidation protocol; see Sections 4.4 and 4.5).The original version of this article has been updated.The first axis of the methodological synthesis erroneously read: "yielding predictive performance that is statistically comparable with-and on several minority-class metrics superior to-strong tabular baselines such as logistic regression, random forests, and gradient boosting." A correction has been made to this passage: First, a compact, carefully regularized multilayer perceptron is trained on a SMOTE-balanced healthcare cohort under a 5-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, which yields predictive performance within one cross-fold standard deviation of strong tabular baselines such as logistic regression, random forests and gradient boosting.The original version of this article has been updated.The third diagnostic check cited the superseded cross-validated AUC-ROC. The passage erroneously read: "the cross-validated AUC-ROC of 0.934 ± 0.026 obtained on the original (un-resampled) test folds (Section 4.4)." A correction has been made to this passage: …and the cross-validated AUC-ROC of 0.916 ± 0.030 obtained on the original (un-resampled) test folds (Section 4.4, leak-free protocol) confirms that the network does not memorize synthetic patterns.In addition, the record-level relationship between the benchmark and its IBM source was not documented, although it determines whether the IBM dataset can serve as a validation set (see the correction to Section 4.12 below). The following paragraph has been added to Section 3.2.1: Record-level relationship to the IBM source. Quantitatively, after excluding the identifier, the relabeled Department and JobRole fields and the Attrition outcome, the 1,676 benchmark rows correspond to exactly 1,470 distinct underlying profiles of the source IBM dataset: 1,264 occur once and 206 occur twice. Among the 206 duplicated profiles, 62 carry a different Department label and 100 a different JobRole label across their two copies, and 15 carry conflicting attrition labels. Because the IBM records are thus wholly contained within the benchmark, the IBM dataset cannot serve as an independent external-validation set (Section 4.12). To verify that this duplication does not drive our results, we de-duplicated the benchmark to its 1,470 unique profiles and re-ran the full 5-fold cross-validation: every metric changed by less than one cross-fold standard deviation and no conclusion was altered.The original version of this article has been updated.The reported hyperparameter sensitivity was carried over from the superseded ablation. The passage erroneously read: "Deviations of ±1 grid step in any single hyperparameter degrade AUC-PR by no more than 0.05, indicating that the chosen configuration lies in a flat optimum rather than on a sharp ridge." A correction has been made to this passage: Under the leak-free protocol, deviations of ±1 grid step in any single hyperparameter change AUC-PR by no more than 0.04 in absolute value (some variants score marginally higher, none significantly so), indicating that the chosen configuration sits in a flat optimum rather than on a sharp ridge.The original version of this article has been updated.Clarification (i) erroneously read: "The picture changes under the more demanding 5-fold crossvalidation protocol of Section 4.4, in which the DNN attains the highest mean AUC-ROC (0.934) and AUC-PR (0.761); the paired-fold significance tests of Section 4.5 show that none of the differences between the DNN and the three baselines is statistically significant after Holm correction, so the four classifiers are best characterized as statistically comparable on this cohort." A correction has been made to this passage:The picture changes under the more demanding 5-fold cross-validation protocol of Section 4.4: under the leak-free protocol gradient boosting attains the highest mean AUC-ROC (0.943) and AUC-PR (0.752), while the DNN (0.916 / 0.713) lies within one cross-fold standard deviation on both metrics; the paired-fold significance tests of Section 4.5 show that the fold-level contrasts are mostly non-significant after Holm correction, although the higher-powered pooled DeLong test does detect small but significant ROC advantages for logistic regression and gradient boosting. The four classifiers are therefore best characterized as of comparable practical magnitude, with the two strongest baselines retaining a small, statistically significant ROC edge.The original version of this article has been updated.Clarification (ii) erroneously read: "Moreover, under the 5-fold cross-validation protocol, the network's mean recall reaches 0.764 ± 0.081, so the test-split value of 0.575 partly reflects the bad luck of an adverse minority sampling on a single 20% split (only 40 leavers in the test fold). Both observations point to the cross-validated numbers as the more representative summary of the model's minority-class sensitivity and to threshold-aware deployment as the appropriate operating-point strategy in practice." A correction has been made to this passage: Moreover, under the leak-free 5-fold cross-validation protocol the network's mean recall is 0.643 ± 0.095, and the test-split value of 0.575 lies within one cross-fold standard deviation of that mean; the single-split sensitivity is therefore consistent with the model's average behavior (the higher figure of 0.764 reported in the originally published version of this passage was a product of the leaked early-stopping protocol). Both observations point to threshold-aware deployment as the appropriate operating-point strategy in practice, with the cross-validated numbers as the representative summary of average minority-class sensitivity.The original version of this article has been updated.There was a mistake in Table 2 as published. In the 5-fold cross-validation block, the row for the proposed DNN (MLP) was computed under the superseded protocol and erroneously read ACC 0.9087 ± 0.034, Pre 0.5994 ± 0.128, Rec 0.7636 ± 0.081, F1 0.6698 ± 0.109, AUC-ROC 0.9340 ± 0.026, AUC-PR 0.7610 ± 0.091, MCC 0.6252 ± 0.125, which also caused the AUC-ROC and AUC-PR columns of that block to be marked bold for the DNN. The held-out test-set block is unaffected. The corrected Table 2 The original version of this article has been updated.The whole of this subsection was based on the superseded values and stated, among other things, that "the DNN attains the highest cross-validated AUC-PR (0.761) and a recall of 0.764" and that "Gradient Boosting, which dominated the single held-out evaluation, drops to an AUC-PR of 0.752 under crossvalidation, demonstrating that its apparent advantage on a single split was partly due to a favorable sampling of the test set." A correction has been made to this subsection:Under this more demanding protocol the deep network achieves an AUC-ROC of 0.916 ± 0.030, an F1 of 0.660 ± 0.085, an AUC-PR of 0.713 ± 0.101 and an MCC of 0.618 ± 0.095, values that lie within one cross-fold standard deviation of the three baselines on every metric. Gradient Boosting attains the highest cross-validated AUC-ROC (0.943) and AUC-PR (0.752), while the DNN remains within one cross-fold standard deviation on both; Logistic Regression retains the highest recall (0.854). Gradient Boosting, which dominated the single held-out evaluation, is confirmed as the strongest model on this benchmark; the fold-level paired tests are mostly non-significant, but the pooled DeLong test of Section 4.5 does find the ROC advantages of Gradient Boosting and Logistic Regression to be small yet statistically significant. The DNN's per-fold AUC-ROC values, reported in Table 4, range from 0.873 to 0.948, and the corresponding distributions across all four classifiers are visualized in Figure 6, which shows that Gradient Boosting achieves the highest median while the inter-quartile ranges of all four classifiers overlap. Taken together, the single-split and crossvalidated analyses indicate that the four classifiers are of comparable practical magnitude-all pairwise mean gaps are at most 0.03 AUC-ROC points, although the two strongest baselines retain a small, statistically significant ROC edge-and that the choice between them should be driven by operational criteria such as interpretability, deployment complexity and the availability of local explanations, rather than by absolute discriminative power alone.The original version of this article has been updated.There was a mistake in Table 4 as published. The per-fold values for the proposed DNN (MLP) were computed under the superseded protocol and erroneously read 0.897 / 0.923 / 0.962 / 0.955 / 0.933 for AUC-ROC and 0.557 / 0.615 / 0.747 / 0.819 / 0.611 for F1. Independently of the protocol, the Logistic Regression F1 value for Fold 1 was erroneously given as 0.557, which was inconsistent with the printed fold-averaged mean of 0.670 ± 0.046; the correct value is 0.624. The corrected The original version of this article has been updated.There was a mistake in Figure 6 as published. The per-fold AUC-ROC distributions shown in the boxplot were those produced by the superseded run, and the caption stated that the discriminative power of the four classifiers is "statistically comparable in this cohort." The figure has been regenerated from the leak-free per-fold values in the original plotting style. The corrected Figure 6 and its corrected caption appear below. The original version of this article has been updated.The third test was erroneously described as "a paired DeepLIFT-corrected DeLong test," which does not name any existing procedure, the caveat on the attainable Wilcoxon p-value at five folds was missing, and the reported outcome was based on the superseded values ("none of the differences between the DNN and the three baselines reaches significance… This confirms that the four classifiers are statistically comparable on this cohort"). A correction has been made to this subsection:For each pair of classifiers we apply (i) a paired two-sided t-test on the fold-level AUC-ROC and AUC-PR values, (ii) the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank counterpart (with five folds the smallest attainable two-sided p-value is 1/16 = 0.0625, so this test is reported for completeness and cannot reach significance at α = 0.05 by construction), and (iii) a paired DeLong test on the concatenated out-of-fold prediction scores in order to compare ROC curves with proper variance accounting. All p-values are adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm-Bonferroni procedure across the three pairwise contrasts that involve the proposed DNN. The resulting test statistics, recomputed under the leak-free cross-validation protocol and summarized in Table 5, indicate that the fold-level t-and Wilcoxon tests do not reach significance at the conventional α = 0.05 level on either AUC-ROC or AUC-PR, with a single exception (the paired t-test on AUC-PR versus logistic regression, p_adj = 0.039); the higher-powered pooled DeLong test, however, indicates that the small ROC advantages of logistic regression (+0.017, p_adj = 0.011) and gradient boosting (+0.027, p_adj < 0.001) over the DNN are statistically significant, whereas random forest is indistinguishable from the DNN. The four classifiers are therefore of comparable practical magnitude-all pairwise mean differences are at most 0.03 AUC-ROC and 0.04 AUC-PR points-but the DNN should be described as competitive rather than statistically equivalent: the two strongest baselines retain a small, significant ROC edge on this benchmark, which is consistent with the choice, maintained throughout this article, of motivating the deep network by its attribution and extensibility properties rather than by discriminative superiority (Section 4.9), in line with the qualitative conclusion drawn from Figure 6.The original version of this article has been updated.There was a mistake in The original version of this article has been updated.There was a mistake in Table 6 as published. title: Desarrollo de habilidades de pensamiento mediante robótica educativa en educación inicial: una revisión sistemática
abstract: La robótica educativa surgió como una herramienta para potenciar el desarrollo de habilidades de pensamiento en estudiantes de educación inicial, dando paso a que sistemas educativos a nivel mundial acojan enfoques educativos en donde esta tecnología haga parte de sus prácticas, justificando la necesidad de analizar estudios realizados previamente que evidencien la efectividad de esta. Se realizó una revisión sistemática, siguiendo el protocolo PRISMA, en la base de datos Web of Science, y se analizaron finalmente 27 artículos originales. Los resultados se organizaron en tres categorías: pensamiento computacional, pensamiento creativo y robótica educativa, donde se destaca que la robótica favorece el desarrollo de la secuenciación, la resolución de problemas, la abstracción y la creatividad, además de mejorar habilidades lógico-matemáticas, sociales y emocionales. De igual manera, se identificaron aspectos clave como el uso de proyectos con el método STEM, actividades lúdicas que potencien el aprendizaje significativo y la mediación docente, la cual permite una transformación en sus prácticas pedagógicas. La robótica permite un aprendizaje integral, lo que conlleva la necesidad de ser adaptada como un recurso de transformación pedagógica y constituirse en un reto que debe ser atendido desde la investigación pedagógica, la práctica docente y la política pública.

title: Generative AI-Based Visual Reading Materials for Adults with Intellectual Disabilities: A Preliminary Evaluation with Adults without Disabilities
abstract: Objectives: This study developed reading materials for adults with intellectual disabilities using generative AI and, prior to testing these materials with the target population, examined differences in perceived ease of comprehension, perceived comprehension efficiency, and material appropriateness across three conditions (original text, AI-converted text, AIconverted text with images) among adults without disabilities. Methods: Fifteen reading materials (5 domains×3 conditions) were developed across five domains—Income & Welfare, Medical & Health, Employment, Residential & Daily Living, and Civic Participation—under three conditions: original text (condition 1), AI-converted text (condition 2), and AIconverted text with images (condition 3). Prompts followed Easy-to-Read guidelines and Korean vocabulary grade standards from the National Institute of Korean Language, and content validity was confirmed by three speech-language pathologists. Twenty-eight adults without disabilities rated each condition using a 5-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using the Friedman test with Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon post-hoc tests; effect sizes were calculated using Kendall’s W. Results: Perceived ease of comprehension showed no significant differences among conditions. Perceived comprehension efficiency differed significantly only between conditions 1 and 3. Material appropriateness differed significantly across all three conditions, with ratings increasing progressively from condition 1 to condition 2 to condition 3. Conclusion: In this preliminary evaluation with adults without disabilities, material appropriateness and perceived comprehension efficiency received relatively higher ratings in condition 3 compared to condition 1. These findings indicate that adults without disabilities perceived AI-transformed materials, including those supplemented with images, as relatively appropriate. Future studies should objectively examine the actual reading comprehension of adults with intellectual disabilities.

title: Development and temporal validation of a proof-of-concept artificial intelligence model for binary classification of cervical cotest
abstract: To develop and temporally validate a proof-of-concept deep learning model applied to digitized ThinPrep cervical cytology and human papillomavirus (HPV) cotest results for cervical dysplasia identification and triage support. This retrospective single-center study included women undergoing cervical cotesting at Fondazione IRCCS Istituto Nazionale dei Tumori, Milan, Italy, between January and September 2023 (development cohort January-July; temporal validation cohort August-September). The model distinguished true-negative cotest cases from HPV-positive low-grade/high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions; atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance or cannot exclude high-grade lesion, glandular abnormalities, and invasive lesions were excluded. Two convolutional neural network architectures (ResNet50 and DenseNet201) were trained using transfer learning and evaluated by three-fold cross-validation. The best-performing model was validated on an independent temporal cohort (732 image patches; n = 63 women). ThinPrep slides from 337 women generated 3867 image patches for model development. All performance metrics are reported at the image-patch level and not at the patient level. The ResNet50 ensemble achieved the highest patch-level performance (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve: 96%) in temporal validation. At the optimized 30% threshold, sensitivity was 93%, negative predictive value 94%, and accuracy 89%. Reference cotest categories were significantly associated with colposcopic impression (P < 0.001) and histological outcome (P < 0.001 in the development cohort). The model demonstrated high patch-level discriminative ability for the selected binary cotest classification. Although these findings suggest a potential role for artificial intelligence-assisted cytology within screening programs, prospective multicenter studies with patient-level analysis are required before clinical implementation.

title: Geometry-Dependent Bounds for Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization
abstract: We study adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets. A learner commits each action before observing its objective and competes with the best fixed action in hindsight. We prove a comparator-uniform first-order inequality that gives coefficient $4/9$, improving the online $0.401$ benchmark, with one gradient query and one projection per round and $O(\sqrt T)$ expected approximate regret. If $ζ{\bf 1} \in K\subseteq[0,1]^d$, the coefficient improves to $\underlineα(ζ)=\tfrac12-(1-2ζ)_+^2/[2(3-2ζ)^2]$. The proof is a direct ordered-coordinate argument with an objective-independent rational action. Conversely, a three-group symmetry-gap construction yields an offline oracle upper bound $β_*=0.470438681380894\ldots$ at $ζ=0$, even with exact value and full-gradient responses. A parameterized extension and exact finite-instance bounds define an upper function for every $ζ$. The lower and upper bounds match at $1/2$ for $ζ\ge1/2$, and show that the optimal deficit from $1/2$ is $Θ((1/2-ζ)^2)$ as $ζ\uparrow1/2$. For coefficient-revealed polynomials we obtain $1/2$ for quadratics and a geometry-dependent cubic coefficient starting at $8/17$, including $0.49$ at $ζ=1/5$. A constant objective sequence yields an offline $(4/9-\varepsilon)$ approximation with polynomially many first-order queries on the cube and projections, without requiring a supplied positive lower bound on the optimum. We also give nonanticipating adaptive-adversary and value-feedback guarantees, including $O(T^{3/4})$ regret with one noisy value per round.

title: Measuring LLM Agent Defenses by Layer: GDA Measurement and an Envelope-Layer Attack-Defense Model
abstract: Agent interaction protocols such as ACP and A2A let a remote peer deliver a task the receiving agent treats as legitimate, opening a channel for indirect prompt injection. Evaluating and defending such agents is difficult because the attack success rate (ASR) cannot distinguish an LLM recognition failure from an agent-layer block, and so cannot indicate which layer to strengthen. We contribute three artifacts. (1) GDA Measurement, a red-team method that captures the raw agent-LLM context at the gateway, preserves conversation and raw-capture data, and judges outcomes autonomously with an agent selected by an inter-annotator-agreement (IAA) study over six candidates; its four classes, A/B/C/D, replace ASR with the semantic refusal, semantic breach, interception and penetration rates - a layer-resolved view of defense. (2) A2A-TIBA, an implant-command-exfiltration principle on A2A that generates this method's validation corpus, designed to spread outcomes across the four classes rather than to maximize the success rate. (3) ELA-ITL, a three-layer isomorphic attack-defense model induced from that corpus, which identifies the envelope layer - the channel through which content enters an agent - as a defense surface; ablating the A2A, tool and memory channels shows that annotating untrusted content markedly improves recognition of malicious content.

title: Quantum Log-Determinant Methods for Torsion-Sensitive Topological Data Analysis
abstract: Betti numbers are central to topological data analysis but fail to capture torsion in integral homology. Torsion can distinguish topological structures with identical Betti numbers, and examples from classical topological data analysis show that it can affect the topology inferred from data. Related torsion-sensitive quantities are also known to have practical applications in graph-based machine learning, including biomedical applications. We investigate how quantum spectral methods can access this additional information. Log pseudodeterminants, obtained by summing the logarithms of the nonzero boundary-Laplacian eigenvalues, summarize spectral information about a simplicial complex. Under explicit topological assumptions, an alternating combination of these quantities gives the size of a higher critical group, the higher-dimensional analogue of a graph sandpile group. With stronger certification, a related construction recovers the size of the torsion subgroup in homology itself. This is, to our knowledge, the first provably correct quantum estimator of integral-homology torsion order. We give a new quantum algorithm for estimating these quantities, with explicit dependence on how the input is queried, the required accuracy, and the spectral gaps. Exact spectra for balanced multipartite clique complexes provide favorable gaps, and a related construction gives an explicit torsion-bearing benchmark. With compact query access, the algorithm need not construct the exponentially large boundary matrices explicitly. For a restricted torsion-bearing family, a tailored amplitude-estimation routine uses quadratically fewer queries than any randomized classical algorithm given comparable access when estimating the log pseudodeterminant. Estimating the full, unnormalized quantity to fixed additive error still costs in proportion to the candidate-space dimension $D$.

title: Natural Barriers to Quantum Extraction: On the Post-Quantum (In)security of (O)EKE and Masny-Rindal OT
abstract: Encrypted key exchange (EKE), introduced by Bellovin and Merritt (IEEE S\&P 1992), and Masny-Rindal OT, introduced by Masny and Rindal (ACM CCS 2019), are highly-efficient methods for compiling essentially any KEM into advanced cryptographic protocols, namely password-authenticated key exchange (PAKE) and oblivious transfer (OT), by relying only on idealized symmetric-key primitives. They have become leading candidates for practically-implementable PAKE and OT due to (1) their simplicity, (2) their plug-and-play nature, allowing for flexibility in the choice of KEM, and (3) existing proofs of UC-security (in the classical adversarial model). Due to point (2) above, these compilers yield attractive candidates for efficient \emph{post-quantum} PAKE and OT, especially given the recent post-quantum KEM standardization efforts. This motivates the question of whether the (UC-)security of these compilers translates to the quantum adversarial model. In this work, we show that it does not. In particular, we prove that a general family of (O)EKE protocols, as well as Masny-Rindal OT, are \emph{not} UC-secure against quantum polynomial-time adversaries, even when instantiated with a post-quantum KEM. To establish UC-insecurity, we devise an adversarial strategy that provably thwarts any attempt by the simulator to extract its input (the password in the case of PAKE, and the receiver's choice bit in the case of OT). To complement these negative results, we establish that both compilers yield certain notions of \emph{game-based} security. Along the way, we establish a novel ``advantage-tight'' one-way to hiding lemma that may be of independent interest.

title: ExpandDiff: Dynamic Range Expanding Diffusion for Single-Image HDR Reconstruction
abstract: Single-image HDR reconstruction requires inferring missing detail while preserving the visible content of an LDR image. Differences in sensor dynamic range and exposure cause LDR images to lose varying amounts of information in shadows and highlights. We present ExpandDiff, a conditional diffusion pipeline that jointly reconstructs clipped shadows and highlights. To account for this variation, we introduce Dynamic Clipping Synthesis (DCS), which randomly samples shadow and highlight clipping percentiles when constructing training inputs from HDR targets. A pixel-space diffusion model guided by spatially-adaptive normalization then predicts perceptually encoded HDR through a bounded output head, reconstructing both clipping directions in one sampling trajectory. On the SI-HDR benchmark, ExpandDiff variants improve HDR reconstruction accuracy by 3.43 dB in PU21-PSNR over the strongest evaluated competing method, and by 7.34 dB under two-sided clipping. The code and supplementary material are available at https://memreandiran.github.io/expanddiff/.

title: Search Shapes Conclusions: Auditing Evidence Selection Bias in Deep Research Agents
abstract: Deep Research agents synthesize evidence into cited reports, yet a well-cited report can still reach a misleading conclusion. Citation correctness checks whether cited sources support individual claims. It does not show whether adaptive search exposed a representative view of all documents made available for evaluation, which we call the candidate pool. Early findings redirect later queries, document choices, and stopping, so the documents an agent reads form a selective sample. Existing evaluations rarely account for this selection. We formulate the problem as adaptive evidence sampling and introduce Causal Evidence Selection Correction (CESS). CESS predicts each candidate document's evidence direction and corrects the candidate-pool average using the logged probabilities of selecting each document and reaching each search round. Shrinkage stabilizes short searches, while intervals replace point estimates when some documents cannot be sampled. We also prove that estimating the average evidence direction of a common pool differs from measuring how a change in search policy alters the evidence read. The latter requires intervention. On questions from the MS2 systematic-review benchmark, CESS reduces mean absolute error against the candidate-pool average by $9.2\%$ and reduces the estimate's change under opposing document rankings by $39.4\%$ relative to averaging the evidence scores of documents read. Across trajectories from a public Open Deep Research agent, the corresponding reductions reach $60.1\%$ and $87.2\%$. A further 4,800 trajectories under paired interventions confirm that correcting a pool estimate and measuring a policy effect are different tasks. CESS therefore audits whether the evidence direction underlying a report reflects the documents available for evaluation, while a separate intervention analysis measures the effect of search decisions.

title: Lightweight Cryptographic Algorithms in IoT Communication: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: This review describes the lighting description language used for lightweight cryptographic algorithms. This paper focuses on a simple problem. How can small IoT devices protect data when power, memory and computing power are low? In the story, the meaning and main types of lightweight cryptography are explained. In addition, it also introduces the common usage in RFID system, wireless sensor networks and smart grids. This review compares LED, PRESENT and KTANTAN. These algorithm will reduce the cost and energy consumption, but there are still attack problems such as fault attacks and side-channel attacks. The paper also discusses the reuse of hardware, the design of composite field, the simplification of software and parallel processing. The last part is 5G, edge computing, attribute-based encryption and hybrid encryption. The main results are clear. Although Lightweight cryptography contributes to the security of IoT, every design needs to be fully tested and continuously improved.

The paper also discusses the reuse of hardware, the design of composite field, the simplification of software and parallel processing. The last part is 5G, edge computing, attribute-based encryption and hybrid encryption. The main results are clear. Although Lightweight cryptography contributes to the security of IoT, every design needs to be fully tested and continuously improved.

title: Sentiment Analysis of User Reviews for the BCA Mobile App on the Google Play Store Using the Random Forest Algorithm
abstract: BCA Mobile adalah salah satu aplikasi perbankan seluler yang populer di Indonesia. Ulasan dari pengguna di Google Play Store dapat digunakan untuk mengevaluasi kepuasan serta keluhan konsumen mengenai fitur aplikasi. Namun, banyaknya ulasan yang ada membuat analisis manual menjadi kurang efisien. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk melakukan analisis sentimen terhadap ulasan pengguna BCA Mobile di Google Play Store dengan menggunakan algoritma Random Forest. Dataset yang digunakan terdiri dari 2.641 ulasan yang diambil melalui scraping dan kemudian diproses melalui beberapa tahapan preprocessing seperti pembersihan, pengubahan huruf besar-kecil, pemisahan kata, penghapusan kata tidak penting, stemming, dan pembobotan TF-IDF. Setelah itu, data diklasifikasikan menjadi sentimen positif, negatif, dan netral dengan menggunakan algoritma Random Forest. Hasil evaluasi model menggunakan confusion matrix menunjukkan nilai accuracy sebesar 78,45%, precision sebesar 79,01%, recall sebesar 78,45%, dan F1-score sebesar 77,92%. Hasil ini menunjukkan bahwa algoritma Random Forest efektif dalam mengklasifikasikan sentimen ulasan pengguna BCA Mobile dengan kinerja yang memuaskan, sehingga dapat memberikan wawasan tentang pandangan pengguna dan menjadi dasar evaluasi bagi pengembang untuk meningkatkan kualitas layanan aplikasi.

title: Data and code for: New bounds on the minimum distance of binary LCD codes of dimensions 7 to 10
abstract: This record contains the data and code accompanying the manuscript "New bounds on the minimum distance of binary LCD codes of dimensions 7 to 10". It provides explicit generator matrices of 141 binary LCD codes with 7 ≤ k ≤ 10 and 51 ≤ n ≤ 256 that improve the best previously known lower bounds on the minimum distance, where the baseline consists of all published codes closed under the known propagation rules. It also provides the upper bound implied by previously published results, 25 further upper bounds obtained from a Gauss-sum linear program with even-subcode constraints and certified in exact rational arithmetic, and the 78 values of dLCD(n,k) that are determined for the first time. All codes can be re-verified (LCD property and exact minimum distance) with two independent verifiers, and all bounds can be recomputed with a single script (src/check_all.py). Version 1.1.0 corrects the comparison baseline of version 1.0.0 (see CHANGELOG.md). Code in src/ is licensed under the MIT License; data in codes/ and data/ are licensed under CC BY 4.0.

title: TapGuard: Temperature-Calibrated Execute–Confirm–Block Routing for LLM-Powered Mobile Agents
abstract: Large language model-powered mobile agents can compose messages, manage files, operate financial applications, and act on content from other applications. Binary allow-or-refuse safeguards fit this setting poorly: some requests are safe to execute, some require confirmation, and some should be blocked. TapGuard is a task-level pre-execution router combining a compact semantic encoder, temperature-scaled three-class probabilities, a fixed rule floor, and confidence-triggered confirmation. Experiments used 150 canonical MobileSafetyBench release 3 tasks and 100 paired action-hint variants under instruction-template and task-category holdout protocols. Under template holdout, TapGuard lowered severity-weighted direct-execution exposure from 35.7% for the MiniLM semantic classifier to 27.7%, while low-risk direct execution declined from 64.0% to 54.0%. The frozen-cue router achieved still lower exposure but directly executed only 18.0% of low-risk tasks. TapGuard increased severe-risk blocking relative to MiniLM without achieving the highest three-way macro-F1. Category holdout showed the same broad trade-off. Privacy, offensiveness, and image-linked cases remained difficult, and generalization to unseen injection patterns was not established. These findings support evaluating mobile safety routing through both protection and preserved automation.

title: Research on Microgrid Optimal Scheduling Based on the Salp Swarm Algorithm
abstract: To address uneven population distribution and premature convergence of the standard Salp Swarm Algorithm (SSA) in grid-connected microgrid scheduling, this study develops an Improved Salp Swarm Algorithm (ISSA). Sine chaotic mapping is used for population initialization. A distance-adaptive follower update is then employed, in which the weight is determined by the normalized distance between an individual and the current best solution, and an acceptance-based Lévy perturbation is applied to the best solution to enhance escape from local optima. The resulting ISSA is applied to a microgrid scheduling model that minimizes economic operation and environmental costs. Benchmark function and microgrid case studies are used to evaluate optimization accuracy, convergence behavior and scheduling feasibility.

title: Komparasi Kinerja Algoritma Machine Learning Untuk Analisis Sentimen Multi-Kelas Pada Data Teks Digital Terhadap Kebijakan Pemerintah
abstract: The development of social media and digital platforms has increased the number of public opinions on various government policies, including the Free Nutritional Meals (MBG) program. Digital text data generated by the public contains important information regarding public perceptions and sentiments, however the characteristics of unstructured data and large data volumes pose challenges in the analysis process. In addition, the integrity of class sentiment can also affect the performance of model classification. This study aims to compare the performance of several Machine Learning algorithms, namely Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, Decision Tree, and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) in multi-class sentiment analysis classification on digital text data related to the MBG program. The dataset used is 4,969 text data from Kaggle in the form of public comments on social media related to government policies. The research method is through data collection, text preprocessing, TF-IDF feature weighting, model training, and evaluation using a confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The preprocessing stages include case folding, tokenizing, stopword removal, and stemming to clean and normalize the text data. Sentiment classification was performed into three categories: positive, negative, and neutral. The results showed that the Random Forest algorithm performed best with an accuracy of 0.81, compared to SVM (0.77), Decision Tree (0.75), Naive Bayes (0.71), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) (0.52). Furthermore, Random Forest also produced higher precision, recall, and F1-score values for most sentiment classes, making it more effective in recognizing sentiment patterns in digital text data on government policies related to the MBG program.

title: Collapse, Not Invariance: Diagnosing Auxiliary Objectives in Speech Anti-Spoofing
abstract: Speech anti-spoofing countermeasures degrade when the generator, codec or channel changes, and a common remedy is an auxiliary objective that shapes the embedding space; whether it does is invisible to EER, a pure ranking metric. We compare seven such objectives with cross-entropy over 113 runs on five corpora, AASIST3 at three seeds plus four pre-trained detectors, and measure the embedding space of the 24 AASIST3 runs directly. Raw augmentation displacement makes cosine consistency look effective, but the gain is a smaller space, not a more stable one: normalised by the spread, no configuration consistently improves on cross-entropy. Every trained space is dominated by the single decision axis expected for two classes, whose training-set structure does not transfer, and four runs collapse to a near-constant output that displacement rewards and EER reports as poor accuracy. No auxiliary objective keeps an advantage over cross-entropy across architectures, corpora and seeds.

title: Semantic Watermarking for Malicious Image Manipulation Detection
abstract: The proliferation of high-fidelity generative editing models has made it possible to inject violent or sexual content into otherwise ordinary images while preserving visual plausibility, with concrete consequences for public discourse and vulnerable populations. We propose a robust semantic watermarking framework that reframes the watermark as a recoverable semantic reference rather than an opaque identifier. Our framework combines a $β$-VAE-based binary watermark (CLIP-VAE) with explicit channel-aware training---random bit-flip noise is injected during training so that the decoder learns graceful degradation under the noisy watermarking channel. As a downstream application, a lightweight module SDA-Net uses the recovered semantic embedding to expose not only whether but in which semantic direction an image has been altered. In a 5-way comparison against representative binary hashing baselines (SimHash, ITQ, HashNet, and their robust-MLP variants), CLIP-VAE achieves the highest reconstruction cosine similarity to the original CLIP embedding under realistic InstructPix2Pix bit-error rates, and uniquely supports direction-of-drift detection---a forensic complement to existing content-moderation pipelines.

title: Low-Discrepancy Dither for Quantized Recurrent State Caches
abstract: Mamba-style and hybrid language models compress their past into a fixed-size recurrent state that is rewritten at every generated token. Storing this state in low precision saves memory bandwidth, but every rounding error is fed back into the next update and can accumulate over long generations. Production systems round the state stochastically; we ask which rounding rule such caches should use. We find that a deterministic golden-ratio Weyl dither, which needs no random numbers, consistently brings the quantized model closer to the full-precision one than stochastic rounding, across pure and hybrid models, storage formats, and long decoding horizons, at no extra cost. Round-to-nearest behaves differently: because it discards small updates, its error keeps growing, so it can look best in short evaluations yet falls far behind over long generations. A discrepancy analysis explains this ordering, and we document implementation pitfalls that silently remove the benefit.

title: A Rank Graduation metric for Algorithmic fairness
abstract: Fairness assessment in algorithmic decisions that affect individuals, such as credit scoring, often relies on parity measures calculated at the aggregate group level. Such measures may not reveal which individuals experience unfairness or which explanatory factors contribute to it. In this paper, we propose a rank-based framework that evaluates fairness through the distribution of model prediction errors, thereby linking fairness assessment with predictive accuracy and explainability. The framework combines Rank Graduation Fairness (RGF), its integrated measure AURGF, a centered Cramer--von Mises permutation test, and a feature removal procedure for fairness explainability. We evaluate the methodology using logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting, and a multilayer perceptron. The simulation study shows that protected-group imbalance can reverse descriptive fairness comparisons, whereas the proposed inferential procedure correctly distinguishes fair from unfair mechanisms. Its application to HMDA mortgage data produces model rankings that differ from those obtained with classical fairness criteria. Tree-based models, rather than logistic regression, provide the strongest combination of predictive accuracy and rank-based fairness, while the fairness null hypothesis is rejected for all four models. The persistence of disparity across statistical, bagging, boosting, and neural network specifications, together with the feature removal results, indicates that the observed unfairness is not specific to a single algorithm or predictor, but is associated with group differences embedded in the characteristics of the lending data. These findings support a broader approach to trustworthy artificial intelligence that combines predictive accuracy, fairness measurement, statistical inference, and explainability.

title: Quantum cryptography and its application in the financial domain: A systematic literature review
abstract: The conventional cryptographic systems that underpin the world's financial infrastructure are under grave threat as quantum computing spreads. The financial industry must immediately investigate quantum-safe alternatives, as widely used public-key algorithms such as RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) are theoretically susceptible to Shor's quantum algorithm, while symmetric schemes face reduced security margins under Grover's algorithm. The Systematic Literature Review (SLR) presented in this paper was carried out in compliance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched using Boolean keywords to find articles published between 2013 and 2025. 53 high-quality studies were chosen from an original corpus of N = 1,654 publications utilizing the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), systematic screening, and eligibility evaluation. Three main paradigms for quantum cryptography were found: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), which includes the NIST-standardised lattice-based algorithms CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium (NIST, 2022); Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), which offers information-theoretic security through the BB84, E91, and CV-QKD protocols; and hybrid quantum-classical architectures that combine near-term deployment with long-term quantum resilience. The operational viability of quantum-secure financial communication has been confirmed through real-world deployments by JPMorgan Chase, HSBC, CaixaBank, and Danske Bank. Given the 'harvest now, decrypt later' (HNDL) threat paradigm, the evidence clearly shows that upgrading to quantum-safe cryptography is an essential operational necessity. Complementary approaches with different trade-offs in cost, scalability, and implementation maturity include QKD, PQC, and hybrid frameworks. To protect the integrity of international financial systems, financial regulators and institutions must coordinate faster adoption roadmaps aligned with NIST PQC standardisation timelines.

title: FROM ARTICLES TO TAGS: Semantic Tagbots Powered by GenAI
abstract: Information management and knowledge organization face the challenge of transforming unstructured textual content into consistent, retrievable metadata semantically linked to domain-specific vocabularies. In digital health contexts, this challenge is intensified by terminological variation, secondary subject mentions, and varying levels of informational relevance. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offer promising alternatives for the extraction, classification, and semantic standardization of textual entities. This paper presents a methodological approach for developing semantic tagbots supported by GenAI, evaluated through a case study on the Afya Portal. The applied problem consists of establishing semantic links between portal articles and an internal disease taxonomy based on the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision (ICD-11). The methodology adopts Design Science Research, comprising iterative cycles of artifact construction, refinement, and evaluation, with successive improvements in the criteria for extraction, scoring, selection, and standardization of tags. Results indicate that combining automated extraction, explicit relevance criteria, and approximation to a domain taxonomy can generate more consistent metadata for information retrieval. As a contribution, the study proposes a methodological process adaptable to other informational contexts requiring the semantic organization of textual content. Conference abstract published in the proceedings of TOI2026 — XII Congresso Internacional em Tecnologia e Organização da Informação. ISSN 2965-4130. Original publication in Doity

abstract: PASTDOOR examines post-exploitation state transformation beyond Apple’s BlastDoor message-parsing boundary. Rather than treating parser containment as the end of the exploit surface, the paper traces how accepted semantic state can continue into trusted system services that serialize, reconstruct, synchronize, allocate, render, transmit, and otherwise act upon it. The analysis follows downstream mechanisms spanning protobuf and XPC materialization, identity and device-state handling, pairing and synchronization, ImageIOXPC, IOSurface, Metal and Metal Performance Shaders, networking telemetry, and accessory-update services. Recovered implementation diagnostics identify concrete validation and failure surfaces involving serialization consistency, XPC interface reconstruction, cryptographic identity state, graphics-resource allocation and lifetime, texture and region constraints, and accessory protocol state. Runtime artifacts provide corresponding observations across downstream platform domains.PASTDOOR models these transitions in terms of reachability, transformation, and authority, distinguishing semantic-state continuity from representation identity. It further examines local retention, authoritative reconstruction, and hybrid reconstruction across lifecycle boundaries. The resulting analysis demonstrates that BlastDoor can constrain parsing authority without containing the lifetime of accepted semantic state: downstream trusted consumers may reconstruct that state under new representations, invariants, and authority. The work is intended for exploit-development, systems-security, digital-forensics, and runtime-systems research.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Sustainable Development: Opportunities, Innovations, and Systemic Risks
abstract: Abstract The paper considers the SDGs as a broad organizing framework, with particular attention to SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 15 (Life on Land). The outcomes of AI applications may vary with local infrastructure, data quality, energy sources, water availability, and institutional capacity. Any numerical claims drawn from prior studies should therefore be interpreted in the context and scope of the original source. This paper is a qualitative review based on secondary information and published literature concerning AI and sustainable development. It uses a descriptive and thematic approach to organize the discussion into application areas, enabling technologies, potential benefits, and implementation risks. The principal themes are precision agriculture, renewable energy integration, circular logistics, data infrastructure, algorithmic fairness, and environmental governance. No new field survey, experiment, or original statistical dataset was collected for this paper. Accordingly, the discussion is interpretive and should not be treated as a causal or quantitative evaluation of a particular AI system.

title: A Data-Driven Graph Model Approach to ICU Patient Trajectory Prediction
abstract: Digital medicine, driven by the increasing adoption of Electronic Health Records (EHRs), enables comprehensive longitudinal tracking of patient health indicators. These indicators are routinely measured and collected by various devices to monitor patient health status, offering valuable insights for clinical decision-making. This project focuses on estimating the correlations and causal relationships among key health indicators in order to enhance patient trajectory prediction, ultimately improving patient care outcomes. We developed a comprehensive analysis pipeline that leverages EHR data to investigate trends and causal relationships among vital health indicators across patient populations. By analyzing the temporal patterns in vital health indicators, we identified distinct patient clusters with similar health trajectories. For each cluster, we implemented a structural equation model (SEM) to capture both intra-time and inter-time dependencies among variables, providing a deeper understanding of the dynamic relationships within each group. To estimate the parameters within these models, we applied an optimization-based method to compute the autoregressive matrices, encapsulating the intra-time and inter-time dependencies. Additionally, we utilized Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) to visualize the causal and correlative relationships among the indicators, offering an intuitive representation of the interactions between vital health metrics. This integrated approach of clustering, SEM, matrix estimation, and DAG visualization enables more accurate modeling of patient health trajectories, yielding predictive insights that are tailored to specific patient cohorts. This framework has the potential to guide more personalized and effective interventions, ultimately improving patient care outcomes.

title: Physics-Informed Gaussian Process with applications in ODE/PDE parameter estimation
abstract: Parameter estimation for nonlinear dynamic system models, represented by ordinary differential equations (ODEs) or partial differential equations (PDEs), using noisy and sparse experimental data is a vital task in many fields. We propose a fast and accurate method, physics-informed Gaussian process, for this task. Our method uses a Gaussian process model over system components, explicitly conditioned on the physics information that gradients of the Gaussian process must satisfy the ODE/PDE system. By doing so, we completely bypass the need for numerical integration and achieve substantial savings in computational time. Our method is also suitable for inference with unobserved system components and provides uncertainty quantification. Our method is distinct from existing approaches as we provide a principled statistical construction under a Bayesian framework, which rigorously incorporates the ODE/PDE system through conditioning. Ref: PIGP for ODE: https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.2020397118 PIGP for PDE: https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/22M1514131

title: SCALE-AWARE ANALYTICAL RADIAL MAPPING VIA TWO-STEP NORMALISATION FOR INTERPRETABLE NONLINEAR FEATURE GENERATION
abstract: Context. The study considers the task of generating an informative and interpretable space of nonlinear features for subsequent use in machine learning models. The object of the study is the process of nonlinear feature generation in tabular data analysis tasks. The basic scheme of such mapping, based on the cosine projection of normalised vectors, provides a simple and computationally efficient way to generate new features. However, this scheme weakens information about the absolute magnitude of input objects. As a result, the informativeness of the transformed space may be limited in tasks where both directional and scale characteristics of the data are important.Objective. The paper aims to improve the analytical radial mapping method for generating an informative space of nonlinear features with a clear geometric interpretation, in which both structural and scale properties of input data are simultaneously taken into account.Method. The basic analytical radial mapping method is improved in the paper by combining cosine-radial feature generation with two-step normalisation and the introduction of an additional scale component into the data representation space. In the first step, column-wise scaling of input features is performed, which ensures alignment of their numerical ranges. In the second step, an extended normalised representation of the object is formed, which contains both the directional structure of features and the integral magnitude characteristic of the vector. After this, a system of centres is defined in the extended space, and new features are determined as cosine similarities between normalised objects and the corresponding prototypes. Unlike the basic approach, the new scheme changes the geometry of the mapping space and allows the transition from a purely directional description to a representation in which the configurational and scale properties of input data are simultaneously preserved.Results. The developed method has been implemented in software and investigated for solving regression tasks on different datasets. The experimental results confirmed the efficiency of the proposed approach and demonstrated that the improved analytical radial mapping forms an informative feature space suitable for accurate prediction with linear regressors.Conclusions. The analytical radial mapping method is improved in the paper by transitioning to an extended data representation space, in which new features are generated taking into account not only the angular proximity to prototypes but also the scale characteristics of objects. Such improvement of the basic method does not reduce to a formal substitution of one normalisation procedure for another, but changes the way the intermediate space is formed, in which cosine similarities to prototypes are subsequently computed.

title: Characterization and prediction of solar radiation in the municipality of Mompox-Bolívar using time series models
abstract: Objective: Considering the growing transition towards renewable energies and specifically the solar potential of Colombia and the Caribbean region with respect to photovoltaic solar energy, as well as the need to develop solar potential characterization studies, in this article, the adjustment and evaluation of four stationary and seasonal time series models (ARIMA, SARIMA, SARIMAX, and Exponential Smoothing) on solar radiation data from the municipality of Mompox-Bolívar are proposed as a contribution. Methodology: Methodologically, within this research, the CRISP-DM methodology was adapted into 4 phases, namely: F1. Business and data understanding, F2. Data preparation, F3. Modeling, F4. Model evaluation and deployment. Results: As a result, it was obtained that at the level of stationary models, the ARIMA (3,0,3) model was the one that achieved the best fit, with a moderate coefficient of determination for the training and test sets. Likewise, with respect to models with a seasonal component, it was determined that the SARIMA model based on ARIMA (3,0,3) and with a seasonal component (1,0,1,8) had the best performance, with a good fit on the training set (R2 of 0.8571) and test set (R2 of 0.8152). Conclusions: It is concluded that the incorporation of the exogenous variable into the SARIMA model did not improve the SARIMA model's performance, such that the SARIMAX model obtained good performance on the training set and moderate performance on the test set. Likewise, the models obtained in this research are of great utility for the characterization of solar radiation potential, as well as for efficient planning in the deployment of photovoltaic solar energy systems.

title: KASTLE: Knowledge-augmented synthetic text generation with logic-enhanced few-shot learning for domain-specific NLP
abstract: Domain-specific NLP models critically depend on labelled data that is expensive and scarce in expert fields. While large language models can generate synthetic data, they lack mechanisms to enforce domain-specific factual and logical constraints. This paper introduces KASTLE, a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates domain knowledge graphs directly into the synthetic text generation process through a novel constraint-guided attention mechanism. Unlike existing approaches that apply symbolic reasoning as post-hoc filters, KASTLE embeds domain constraints at every decoding step, enabling context-aware knowledge injection under few-shot conditions. The framework features three components: a knowledge-augmented generator with real-time constraint satisfaction, a multi-layer quality filter assessing syntactic, semantic, domain, and factual dimensions, and a meta-learning engine that dynamically optimises the mixing of synthetic and real data. Extensive evaluation across medical, legal, financial, technical, and scientific domains demonstrates that KASTLE achieves an average F1 Score of 89.5, outperforming the strongest baseline (InstructAug) by 9.1 percentage points and the strongest retrieval-augmented baseline (RAG-Enhanced) by 11.2 percentage points while reducing labelled data requirements by at least 80%.

title: Quantum state learning beyond approximate unitary designs
abstract: Approximate unitary designs reproduce the statistics of Haar-random unitaries to a given order and accuracy. Recent constructions realize such designs with logarithmic-depth circuits, enabling shallow measurement protocols for various quantum state-learning tasks while preserving performance. These results raise the question of whether approximate designs can replace exact designs more generally. We show that even exponentially small design error need not preserve the learning guarantees of exact designs. This motivates deriving learning guarantees directly from the measurement circuit structure. For observable estimation with classical shadows, we prove that logarithmic-depth two-layer Clifford circuits yield an unbiased estimator matching the global Clifford variance scaling for every state and Hermitian observable. Beyond observable estimation, this bound allows shallow measurements to retain global Clifford guarantees for other tasks, including setting-efficient tomography, mixed-state metrology, and stabilizer structure learning. We complement these statistical guarantees with a compact, exact tensor-network representation of the inverse shadow channel. When measurement bases are reused, approximate unitary designs of arbitrarily high order need not uniformly match the Haar variance in the many-shot limit. For the all-to-all random two-local circuits considered, doing so requires nearly linear depth. Together, our results reveal the capabilities and limitations of shallow quantum state learning, highlighting the distinction between approximating Haar randomness and reproducing its learning guarantees.

title: SQD-Agent: LLM-driven agentic framework for Quantum Chemistry workflows
abstract: Quantum algorithms and quantum hardware are advancing towards a promising paradigm for scientific applications. However, translating domain-specific problems into executable hybrid quantum-classical workflows remains a significant barrier for application researchers due to the required expertise in quantum algorithms, nuances in quantum programming, and hardware-aware system integration. At the same time, AI and primarily LLM based agents are increasingly capable of interpreting natural-language intent, reasoning over complex workflows, and translating high-level objectives into executable code and building computational pipelines. In this work, we introduce SQD Agent, an LLM-based agentic framework that translates natural-language user intent into executable workflows for Quantum Chemistry applications where algorithms from the Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) family are used. By automating this translation, SQD Agent reduces the level of human expertise and configuration overhead required, thereby simplifying experimentation in hybrid quantum-classical settings for application researchers new to quantum. SQD Agent adopts a modular and extensible architecture that supports seamless integration of heterogeneous quantum backends, classical solvers, and workflow components, ensuring adaptability to rapidly evolving quantum ecosystems. The framework further incorporates interactive capabilities for on-demand profiling, bottleneck analysis, resource optimization, intelligent result caching, and convergence visualization. Key features include quantum chemistry experiments, error mitigation on real quantum hardware, together with analysis of candidate mitigation schemes in terms of their potential error-recovery behavior and computational budget, helping users understand their practical trade-offs and decide which strategies to explore in subsequent experiments.

title: Fiber-Resolved Microstructure Quantification from Multi-Shell Diffusion MRI using Detection Transformers
abstract: Fiber orientation and compartmental microstructure are central to the characterization of white matter tissue in diffusion MRI, yet existing methods either resolve fiber orientations without quantifying microstructure, or quantify microstructure while assuming a fixed number of compartments and a single fiber direction. Nonparametric approaches that recover both require tensor-valued diffusion encoding and computationally expensive Monte-Carlo inversion of an ill-posed inverse Laplace transform. We propose to reframe this problem as an object detection-like task, adopting the Detection Transformer (DETR) architecture to jointly predict mean diffusivity (MD), fractional anisotropy (FA), main fiber direction, and signal fraction for a variable number of compartments per voxel from standard multi-shell diffusion MRI with linear encoding. Hungarian matching during training resolves permutation invariance across compartments. We introduce mean Average Precision as a reproducible benchmark metric. Evaluated on synthetic test data with up to five compartments per voxel, our model achieves $R^2=0.95$ for MD, $R^2=0.88$ for FA, and a median angular error of 4.2°, with performance scaling naturally with compartmental signal fraction.

title: Quantum circuit compilation with constant overhead
abstract: Compiling a continuous gate set to a discrete universal gate set generally incurs an overhead. A circuit composed of $G$ arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates can be $ε$-approximated by a sequence of gates from $\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}$ by replacing each original gate by a sequence of $O(\log(G/ε))$ elementary gates. We show that this overhead can be avoided using adaptivity for polynomial-sized circuits with inverse-polynomial target error, which is optimal.

title: Persistent Watermarking of Text-to-Image Models
abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) generation is gaining increasing popularity with the general public, motivating the development of reliable mechanisms for copyrighting such models given their expensive training costs. An adversary may obtain and reuse a pretrained T2I model without authorization, and then serve a modified version through an API service. Such modifications may arise from ordinary downstream adaptation or deliberate attempts to erase ownership, including input-prompt preprocessing, model fine-tuning, and output post-processing. From the model owner's perspective, a key challenge is therefore to embed trigger data that remain persistent under such changes while preserving the model's normal image-generation capabilities. In this work, we propose a contrastive-style watermarking objective with a term that explicitly encourages the watermarked model to behave differently from the original model on trigger inputs. Experiments show substantially stronger trigger-data persistence than prior methods across a wide range of downstream modifications and deliberate attempts to weaken the watermark, resulting in higher detection rates, often approaching 100% TPR@FPR<$10^{-4}$.

title: METAHEURISTIC VERSUS CLASSICAL OPTIMIZATION FOR MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD ESTIMATION IN LAMBERT–TOPP–LEONE REGRESSION MODELS
abstract: This paper develops a Lambert-Topp-Leone (LTL) regression model for limited responses and explores the use of classical and metaheuristic optimisation strategies for maximum likelihood estimation. Grey Wolf Optimiser (GWO) and Differential Evolution (DE) are compared with BFGS and Nelder-Mead using Monte Carlo simulations with different parameter configurations and sample sizes. The performance is evaluated based on bias, RMSE, likelihood achievement, convergence dependability, and computing time. The results show that BFGS performs well under normal likelihood setups, while GWO and DE become competitive under more challenging parameter choices, showing that neither optimiser is uniformly superior.. An application to the MockJurors data indicates that the four techniques yield roughly the same LTL maximum likelihood solutions, lending support to the employment of metaheuristic algorithms as complementary global-search tools for assessing the numerical stability of LTL regression estimates.

An application to the MockJurors data indicates that the four techniques yield roughly the same LTL maximum likelihood solutions, lending support to the employment of metaheuristic algorithms as complementary global-search tools for assessing the numerical stability of LTL regression estimates.

title: Rahnuma: a working guide to the ILM, PANINI and Zistgah stack, from bytes and scripts to compilers, Pāṇini and quantum substrates
abstract: Rahnuma is a working guide to the ILM, PANINI and Zistgah stack, published as a website, a PDF and a single Markdown file from one source. It maps the public repositories of the zistgah, project-ilm and hindawiai organisations with the DOIs each records, as retrieved from the forge on 29 September 2026, and the dated record of the work. It gives exact set-up commands for Ubuntu, Windows with WSL, native Windows and macOS, a first run of PANINIq with its recorded output, and the containers behind the labs. It writes out the mathematics the work rests on: number representation; ASCII, ISCII, Unicode and UTF-8; writing systems and the conditions for reversible transliteration (Kraft-McMillan and Sardinas-Patterson); Panini's Ashtadhyayi as a formal rewriting system; the compiler pipeline from automata and LR parsing to SSA, dataflow, register allocation, microcode, bootstrapping and trusting trust; CMOS, open chip design, balanced ternary and superconducting qubits; and quantum computing with QAOA, the continuous-time quantum walk and Kuramoto oscillators as an Ising machine, as implemented in PANINIq. It shows how to work on the repositories with any AI under verification, how the estate releases and attests its work, and how the GATE 2027 syllabus maps onto it. Every example shown as executed was executed during the build, and the package's gate re-runs them.

title: 掌控信息论:同源通信基础理论 Mastery Information Theory: Foundations of Same-Source Communication
abstract: This work proposes the Mastery Information Theory, taking "Information = Definition" as its first principle, and constructs a unified foundational theory spanning information origin, communication, computation, and fidelity. Core propositions: Information is not in the carrier; it is in the definition. Communication is not the transfer of content, but triggered docking under relative same-source. Consensus does not come from communication; it arises from constraint identity. Computation is not digital iteration, but same-source decomposition and combinatorial screening. The theory takes same-source as its first-principle cornerstone: Same-Source = Consistent Fineness + Consistent Definition. Fineness is the first attribute of definition. Same-source is the sharing condition of information. Trigger is the operational mechanism that activates shared definitions. From this root, it derives constraint resonance, the trigger capacity theorem, the effective decision space, the complete absolute fidelity theorem, the communication-free theorem, and the tensor-product model of nested computers. Boundaries are explicit: it cannot generate entirely new information from nothing, cannot replace universal Turing computation, cannot break through medium relaxation time, and absolute same-source is physically unattainable. Traditional information theory, traditional computers, and traditional distributed consensus are all special cases of this theory at specific limits. Everything is the unfolding of same-source.

title: FC-HMARL Episode-5000 Multi-Seed Reproducibility Checkpoints
abstract: This record provides the trained model checkpoints associated with the final reproducibility release of the FC-HMARL framework. The archive contains 245 PyTorch checkpoint artifacts corresponding to seven experimental configurations evaluated across five random seeds (11, 22, 33, 44, and 55). All checkpoints correspond to the predefined terminal training checkpoint at episode 5000. The associated final TEST evaluation uses 1,268 test episodes per run, deterministic actions, no gradient updates, no replay-buffer writes, and no checkpoint comparison or reselection using TEST data. Configurations: 1. full 2. no_confidence 3. state_only 4. reward_only 5. concatenated 6. multiplicative 7. no_coordinator The accompanying source code, evaluation outputs, protocol files, and aggregated analysis are available in the FC-HMARL GitHub repository, branch: final-reproducibility-clean. title: Elliptic curve cryptography based secure multi-party computation over discrete algebraic structures
abstract: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) enables mutually distrusting parties to jointly evaluate a function over their private inputs without revealing those inputs to any participant.Classical MPC constructions based on Boolean or arithmetic circuits incur significant computational overhead when deployed over large participant groups, and their security guarantees rest upon hardness assumptions that are vulnerable to quantum adversaries.This paper introduces an elliptic curve cryptography-based secure MPC framework that exploits the algebraic structure of elliptic curve groups over finite fields to construct efficient oblivious transfer extensions, Beaver triple generation, and verifiable secret sharing protocols.The framework models the computation as a directed acyclic graph over the elliptic curve group law, enabling algebraic optimizations that reduce the number of point multiplications required per gate evaluation.Pedersen commitments over the curve group provide unconditionally hiding and computationally binding commitment guarantees, while zeroknowledge proofs of knowledge of discrete logarithms authenticate each party's contribution without information leakage.Security is formalized in the universal composability (UC) framework under the decisional Diffie-Hellman (DDH) assumption in the standard model.Evaluation on benchmark circuits including AES key expansion, SHA-3 compression, and private set intersection demonstrates that the proposed EC-MPC protocol achieves 42.3 ms per gate for a four-party evaluation, outperforming BGW by 52.8% and GMW by 42.9% in identical configurations.The framework scales to 32-party computations with sub-quadratic communication overhead, confirming its practicality for cloud-based secure computation, privacy-preserving machine learning inference, and federated healthcare analytics.

title: Optimasi Menu Diet Personalisasi Bagi Penderita Obesitas Menggunakan Algoritma Genetika
abstract: Abstrak. Artikel ini menyajikan implementasi Algoritma Genetika (GA) untuk automasi penyediaan menu diet 7 hari yang dipersonalisasi bagi penderita obesitas. Sistem menghitung kebutuhan energi harian menggunakan persamaan Harris-Benedict untuk memperoleh Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) dan Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE), kemudian menerapkan defisit kalori 25% untuk menentukan target kalori harian, yang selanjutnya dipecah menjadi proporsi karbohidrat, protein, dan lemak sebagai acuan fungsi fitness pada GA. Kromosom direpresentasikan oleh 105 gen dari 130 jenis makanan Indonesia yang dikelompokkan ke dalam tiga food pool (karbohidrat, protein, sayuran), dengan proses seleksi, crossover, dan mutasi yang dievaluasi melalui pengujian OFAT (One Factor at a Time) serta pengujian cross-profile robustness. Hasil pengujian menunjukkan GA mampu menghasilkan menu diet dengan rata-rata deviasi kalori sebesar 1,46%, protein 2,21%, lemak 1,91%, dan karbohidrat 1,64%, jauh di bawah ambang toleransi yang ditetapkan. Konfigurasi parameter Population Size=300, Generations=500, Crossover Rate=0,8, dan Mutation Rate=0,01 terbukti optimal secara universal untuk berbagai profil pengguna, dengan rata-rata fitness global 0,995650. Penelitian ini membuktikan bahwa Algoritma Genetika efektif dan robust dalam menyelesaikan permasalahan optimasi menu diet personalisasi bagi penderita obesitas.

title: Convergence, Bias, and Fairness in Federated Learning: A Non-Stationary Multi-Armed Bandit Approach for Heterogeneous Client Selection
abstract: In practical federated learning (FL) environments, clients often possess non-IID data, which can degrade model performance and extend convergence times. Effective client selection strategies have emerged as a promising approach to mitigate the challenges posed by statistical heterogeneity across clients. This paper proposes two novel non-stationary multi-armed bandit (MAB) approaches for dynamic client selection, addressing the inherent challenges of time-varying client data distributions and their impact on model performance. Unlike traditional methods that assume stationary reward distributions, our approach adapts to evolving client behaviors and data characteristics, ensuring that selection decisions reflect current relevance rather than outdated information. We evaluate client selection as a trade-off among three critical objectives: 1) Maximizing convergence rate to expedite training, 2) Minimizing solution bias to enhance model generalizability, 3) Promoting fairness to ensure consistently high performance across clients. Leveraging non-stationary MAB techniques, Discounted Upper Confidence Bound (D-UCB) and Sliding Window UCB (SW-UCB), we effectively balance exploration and exploitation to address client variability. Additionally, our method evaluates the potential contributions of each client by dynamically weighting recent data trends, providing an opportunity for under-represented clients to participate. Through comprehensive experiments, we examine the trade-offs between accelerating convergence and reducing bias while maintaining fair performance distribution across clients. The proposed approach provides a robust solution to the nuanced trade-offs inherent in federated client selection.

title: Beyond the Sycophancy Score: How Task, Model, and Pressure Shape LLM Yielding
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often abandon a correct answer, or endorse a user's position, once the user pushes back. This behavior, called sycophancy, is usually reported as a single rate per model, which says little about when it happens or how a user can avoid it. We study the conditions that produce it with 103,939 graded replies from ten configurations: eight LLMs with reasoning disabled, and two of them again with maximum reasoning, all facing the same 200 items, 13 pressure conditions, and four-turn conversations, with every reply labeled by two independent LLM judges. We find that the dominant factors are how costly it is for the model to verify the user's claim, and whether a trained guardrail covers it. Removing this task factor from a logistic model costs 0.485 of McFadden $R^2$, against 0.139 for model family and 0.009 for pressure tactic. Anchored facts are almost never conceded (1.3%), while adoption on logic puzzles rises with the number of clues needed to refute the pushed answer. Personal choices are endorsed in 77.0% of conversations. Most concessions on hard items come from models that cannot reliably solve them; models that can solve them rarely give the answer up. For both models tested, maximum reasoning removes these concessions completely: adoption on deep puzzles falls from 19.2% and 12.5% to 0%. Fallacious or emotional framing adds nothing beyond plain repetition. Three human annotators agree with the judges' consensus on 118/120 calibration items. These results give practical rules for reliable use: simplify hard-to-verify problems and reason deeply, state the question rather than one's preferred answer, ask for evidence on open questions, and choose models by their measured guardrail profile.
